title: ADC and DAC
goals: Work out an ADC's smallest step from its range and number of bits
Turn raw counts back into volts, milliamps and engineering units
Scale a Siemens PLC's analogue value (0 to 27648) to and from engineering units
Choose a sample rate that avoids aliasing, and say what an anti-alias filter is for
Work out the number a DAC or analogue output needs for a given current
summary:
An **ADC** (analogue-to-digital converter) turns a voltage into a **number**; a **DAC** turns a number into a voltage or current. Every PLC analogue card has one or the other.

**Resolution**: an n-bit converter splits its range into $2^n$ steps, each $\frac{V_{range}}{2^n}$. A 12-bit ADC on 0–10 V steps about 2.4 mV; 10-bit on 0–5 V, about 4.9 mV. Any reading is uncertain by about **half a step** (quantisation error), plus noise.

**Back to volts**: $V = \frac{counts}{2^n} \times V_{range}$ (near enough for most work). Then into engineering units with the scaling from the sensors lesson.

**Siemens S7 analogue values**: whatever the converter's bits, the card reports the **nominal range as 0 to 27648**: 0–10 V, 0–20 mA and **4–20 mA** all give 0 at the bottom and 27648 at the top (on a 4–20 mA range, 4 mA reads **0**; on a 0–20 mA range it would read 5530). Above 27648 up to 32511 is **overrange**; 32767 is overflow (broken wire or short, depending on the range). Scale in TIA Portal with **NORM_X** (raw to 0.0–1.0) then **SCALE_X** (to engineering units):

$x = x_{lo} + \frac{raw}{27648}(x_{hi} - x_{lo})$

**Sampling**: an ADC takes readings at a sample rate $f_s$. To capture a signal without **aliasing** (a fast signal appearing as a false slow one), sample at more than **twice** the highest frequency in it: $f_s > 2 f_{max}$ (the **Nyquist** rule), and in practice 5 to 10 times. An **anti-alias filter** (a low-pass filter before the ADC) removes what is too fast to sample.

**DAC / analogue output**: the same scaling backwards: for 4–20 mA on an S7 output card, raw $= \frac{I - 4}{16} \times 27648$.
sources: Siemens: S7-1200 Programmable controller System Manual, appendix: representation of analog values (input and output ranges)
Siemens: TIA Portal help: NORM_X and SCALE_X instructions
Horowitz, P. and Hill, W.: The Art of Electronics, 3rd edition (Cambridge University Press): ADCs, DACs and sampling
Kuphaldt, T. R.: Lessons In Industrial Instrumentation (digital data acquisition, Nyquist and aliasing)

bench.task: On a PLC analogue input you can monitor (or a simulator), compare the raw value with a known signal.
check: Inject 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 mA with a loop calibrator (or read a 0–10 V signal at known points)
Write down the raw value each time: 4–20 mA on a 4–20 mA range should be about 0, 6912, 13824, 20736, 27648
Check the scaled value the program shows against your own sums
Unplug the signal: what does the raw value and the card's diagnostic show?

cards.q: A 12-bit ADC measures 0 to 10 V. Roughly how big is its smallest step?
cards.why: 12 bits give $2^{12} = 4096$ steps: $10 \div 4096 = 0.0024$ V. 0.83 V is 10 ÷ 12, as if each bit were a step.

cards.title: An ADC turns volts into a number
cards.body:
An **ADC** measures a voltage and gives a whole number. An **n-bit** ADC splits its range into $2^n$ steps:

$$\Delta V = \frac{V_{range}}{2^n}$$

More bits, finer steps: 10 bits on 0–5 V is about 4.9 mV a step; 16 bits on 0–10 V is about 0.15 mV.

Any reading is only good to about **half a step** (the **quantisation error**), plus whatever noise is on the signal.
cards.more:
Think of a ruler marked only in whole millimetres: anything in between gets rounded to the nearest mark. The ADC's marks are its steps.

Numbers: an Arduino-style 10-bit ADC on 5 V has $2^{10} = 1024$ steps of $5 \div 1024 = 4.9$ mV. A temperature sensor giving 10 mV per °C is then read to about half a degree.

More bits only help if the signal is clean: a 16-bit ADC with 5 mV of noise on its input still only gives you a reading to about 5 mV.

cards.q: A {n}-bit ADC measures 0 to {vr} V. How big is its smallest step, in mV?
cards.why: The range is split into $2^n$ equal steps.

cards.title: From counts back to volts
cards.body:
To turn a reading back into volts:

$$V = \frac{counts}{2^n} \times V_{range}$$

(Some datasheets divide by $2^n - 1$; the difference is one step, too small to matter for most work.)

Then turn volts into what they stand for, with the scaling from the sensors lesson.
cards.more:
Numbers: a 10-bit ADC on 5 V reads 377. $\frac{377}{1024} \times 5 = 1.84$ V.

If that is a 0–5 V pressure sensor ranged 0–6 bar: $\frac{1.84}{5} \times 6 = 2.2$ bar.

You can skip the volts: the fraction of the range, $\frac{377}{1024} = 0.368$, times 6 bar gives 2.2 bar directly. Most PLC scaling does exactly that.

cards.q: A {n}-bit ADC on 0–{vr} V reads {cnt}. What voltage is that?
cards.why: Counts over the number of steps is the fraction of the range; times the range gives volts.

cards.title: PLC raw values: Siemens' 0 to 27648
cards.body:
PLC cards hide the ADC's bits behind a fixed scale. On **Siemens S7** analogue inputs, the **nominal range** always reads **0 to 27648**:

- 0–10 V: 0 V reads 0, 10 V reads 27648
- 4–20 mA (set as a 4–20 mA range): **4 mA reads 0**, 20 mA reads 27648
- the same 4 mA on a **0–20 mA** range reads 5530

Above 27648 (to 32511) is **overrange**; 32767 flags overflow. Scale with **NORM_X** then **SCALE_X**:

$$x = x_{lo} + \frac{raw}{27648}(x_{hi} - x_{lo})$$
cards.more:
27648 leaves room above the nominal range so the card can still show a value that has gone a bit over, before it flags overflow.

Numbers: a 0–10 bar transmitter on a 4–20 mA range reads 13824. $\frac{13824}{27648} = 0.5$, so 5 bar (and the loop is at 12 mA).

The card's range setting matters: if the card is set to 0–20 mA but the transmitter is 4–20 mA, the live zero reads 5530, not 0, and a scaling that assumes 0 will read 2 bar at zero pressure. Match the card's range to the signal, or allow for it in the scaling.

In TIA Portal: NORM_X(MIN := 0, VALUE := raw, MAX := 27648) gives 0.0–1.0; SCALE_X(MIN := 0.0, VALUE := that, MAX := 10.0) gives bar.

cards.q: A Siemens analogue input (4–20 mA range) reads {raw} from a transmitter ranged 0–{hi} bar. What is the pressure?
cards.why: On its 4–20 mA range the card already takes off the live zero: 0 is 4 mA, 27648 is 20 mA. So raw ÷ 27648 is the fraction of the range.

cards.title: Sampling and aliasing
cards.body:
An ADC takes **samples**: one reading every so often, at a **sample rate** $f_s$.

To capture a signal, sample at more than **twice** its highest frequency (the **Nyquist** rule):

$$f_s > 2 f_{max}$$

Sample too slowly and a fast signal shows up as a false, slower one: **aliasing**. No amount of later processing can undo it.

So a **low-pass anti-alias filter** goes before the ADC, to remove anything too fast to sample. In practice, sample 5 to 10 times faster than the fastest thing you care about.
cards.more:
The classic picture is a wagon wheel in an old film appearing to turn slowly backwards: the camera's frames (samples) catch the spokes a little behind where they were each time.

In a plant: a vibration at 49 Hz sampled 50 times a second looks like a slow 1 Hz wobble. Nothing in the data says it is really 49 Hz.

A PLC analogue card usually filters and averages its readings for you (and the scan time is a sampling rate of its own). That is fine for temperatures and levels, but it means a PLC is the wrong tool for catching fast events or vibration: those need a dedicated DAQ with a proper anti-alias filter.

cards.q: A signal contains nothing above {fm} Hz. What is the lowest sample rate the Nyquist rule allows (it must be more than this)?
cards.why: More than twice the highest frequency. That is a bare minimum; 5 to 10 times gives a usable picture of the wave's shape.

cards.title: DACs and analogue outputs
cards.body:
A **DAC** goes the other way: a number in, a voltage or current out. A PLC's **analogue output** card is a DAC.

On a Siemens S7 output, 0 to 27648 gives the nominal range: for 4–20 mA, 0 gives 4 mA and 27648 gives 20 mA. To send a current $I$:

$$raw = \frac{I - 4}{16} \times 27648$$

The output only changes in steps, and only when the program writes a new value, so it is a staircase, smoothed by the card's own filtering.
cards.more:
Numbers: to send 12 mA (half the range) to a valve positioner: $\frac{12 - 4}{16} = 0.5$; $0.5 \times 27648 = 13824$.

Usually the program works in engineering units: a valve 0–100% open. Then raw $= \frac{\%}{100} \times 27648$, and the card does the 4 mA offset itself. In TIA Portal that is NORM_X then SCALE_X the other way round, or UNSCALE in older blocks.

Check the output with a meter in the loop: 0% should give 4.0 mA, 100% 20.0 mA. If 0% gives 0 mA, the card is set to a 0–20 mA range.

cards.q: A Siemens analogue output is set to 4–20 mA. What raw value makes it send {ma} mA?
cards.why: Fraction of the range (live zero off, ÷ 16), times 27648.
cards.hint: The same scaling as an input, backwards.

cards.q: A level transmitter ranged 0–4 m is wired to a Siemens input set to 4–20 mA. It reads 17280. What is the level, and what current is in the loop?

steps.ask: A check you can do with a meter.
steps.show: Measure the loop: about 14 mA confirms the card and the scaling.

cards.why: Raw to fraction to units; the loop current is the same fraction of the 4–20 mA span. A meter reading that disagrees points at the card's range setting or the wiring.

cards.q: Why is there no '− 4 mA' step when working from the raw value in step 1?
cards.context: Raw 17280 ÷ 27648 = 0.625 of the range, on a 4–20 mA range.
cards.model: On a 4–20 mA range the card itself takes off the live zero: it reports 4 mA as 0 and 20 mA as 27648. So the raw value is already measured from the bottom of the range, and dividing by 27648 gives the fraction directly. Taking off 4 again would be counting the live zero twice. It would only be needed if the card were set to 0–20 mA, where 4 mA reads 5530.

cards.q: A 0–10 V speed signal (0–1500 rpm) goes to a Siemens input set to 0–10 V. It reads 20736. What speed is it?
cards.why: Same move whatever the signal: raw ÷ 27648 for the fraction, then the fraction of whatever the range stands for.

cards.q: A Siemens input on a 0–10 V range reads {raw}. The signal stands for 0–{hi} °C. What temperature is it?
cards.why: Raw over 27648, times the span.

cards.q: A level shows 2.1 m when the dipstick says 2.5 m (range 0–4 m, raw 17280). One line of the scaling is wrong. Which?
cards.why: Siemens cards put the top of the nominal range at 27648, not 32767. Dividing by 32767 reads every value about 16% low. Check with a known current: 20 mA should read exactly the top of the range.

cards.q: A 4–20 mA transmitter is wired to a Siemens input wrongly set to 0–20 mA. What raw value does the input show when the loop is at {ma} mA?
cards.why: On a 0–20 mA range, 0 mA reads 0 and 20 mA reads 27648, so 4 mA reads 5530. A scaling written for 4–20 mA would then show a value at the live zero.

cards.q: A 49 Hz vibration is logged at 50 samples a second. What does the log show?
options: A false slow wobble of about 1 Hz
cards.why: Each sample catches the wave slightly earlier in its cycle, so the samples trace out a slow 1 Hz wave that is not really there: aliasing. To see 49 Hz, sample at well over 98 Hz, with an anti-alias filter.

cards.q: A 0–10 V signal must be read in steps of no more than {mv} mV. How many bits does the ADC need, at least? (Give the whole number.)
cards.work: Steps needed: $\frac{10}{{mv} \times 10^{-3}}$; the smallest $2^n$ at least that: $n = {answer}$
cards.why: Find how many steps the range needs, then the smallest power of 2 that gives at least that many.
cards.hint: How many steps of {mv} mV fit in 10 V? Then which power of 2 covers it?

cards.q: A reading from an ideal 8-bit ADC on 0–5 V (steps of about 19.5 mV) is converted back to volts. Roughly how far could it be from the true voltage?
cards.why: Every reading is rounded to the nearest step, so it can be out by up to half a step: about ±10 mV here. Noise adds to that.

cards.q: A Siemens input on a 4–20 mA range reads {raw}. What is the loop current?
cards.why: The fraction of the range (raw ÷ 27648), then the sensors lesson's rule: 4 mA plus that share of the 16 mA span.
cards.hint: Fraction of the range, then 4 + 16 × fraction.

cards.q: A 16-bit card reads a thermocouple to 0.01 °C on screen, but the reading wanders by ±0.5 °C. What limits the real accuracy?
options: Noise and the sensor, not the ADC's step
cards.why: A fine step only shows more digits; noise, the thermocouple's tolerance and cold-junction error set the real accuracy. Decimals on a screen are not accuracy.

cards.q: A valve's 4–20 mA output (Siemens, 4–20 mA range) must be {pc}% open. What raw value?
cards.why: Working in per cent of the range, the card adds the 4 mA itself: raw = fraction × 27648.

cards.q: A {n}-bit ADC on 0–10 V. Smallest step, in mV?
cards.why: The range over $2^n$ steps.

cards.q: Siemens input (4–20 mA range), raw {raw}, transmitter 0–{hi} m. Level?
cards.why: Raw ÷ 27648 is the fraction of the range.

cards.q: What does an anti-alias filter do?
options: Removes frequencies too fast to sample, before the ADC
Removes noise after the ADC has converted it
Adds more bits to the ADC
cards.why: Once aliased, a false frequency cannot be removed. A low-pass filter before the ADC stops anything faster than half the sample rate getting in.
